Assertion failure reporting and the handlers that receive it. The application decides what a failed check does. setCallbacks() registers a handler that receives the failure description and answers with the toy::assertion::Action the check takes, plus a second handler that receives stack frames. Registration is valid between initialize() and deInitialize(). With no handler registered, a failed check reports nothing and stops at the check. Typical wiring, from the composition root: #include <cstdio> #include "core.hpp" namespace { toy::assertion::Action reportAssertion(const char * assertionString) noexcept { std::fputs(assertionString, stderr); return toy::assertion::Action::Break; } } // namespace int main() { toy::assertion::initialize(); toy::assertion::setCallbacks(reportAssertion, nullptr); // Run the application; in a debug build a failed check reaches reportAssertion() and then breaks. toy::assertion::deInitialize(); return 0; } к сведению A check that must fail the build uses static_assert. Text utilities shared across the core types: character search and comparison, plus UTF-8 and UTF-16 conversion, counting, and validation. A search or comparison function reads only the characters inside the toy::span it is given: it needs no terminator after them, and a '\0' inside counts as an ordinary character. Counting and validation also take a null-terminated string and walk it to its terminator. Characters compare as bytes with no locale, so a result is identical across runs and targets. No function allocates. Search, comparison, and toy::string_utils::utf8Size() work in a constant expression; every other function is a runtime one, defined in a translation unit. A sequence or set search takes O(n * m) comparisons in the worst case, in the length of the range and of the pattern or set; the rest take O(n). Major, minor, and patch numbers of a build, with the revision it was built from. Aggregate the caller fills field by field; every member has a default, so an omitted number reads 0 and an omitted revision holds no characters. The three numbers rank the release. revision names the source of the build, a commit hash or a tag, and settles the order when the numbers match.

Aggregate initialization: no constructor, so designated initializers name the fields at the call site. Constexpr support: construction and both comparisons evaluate in a constant expression. Ordered: equality over all four fields, and a three-way order that reads the numbers first and the revision last. No allocation: three integers and a view; the revision characters belong to whoever created them. Determinism: the order consults no locale and holds across runs and targets. Exception safety: no operation throws; exceptions are off in the build.
#include "application.hpp" const toy::application::Version build{1, 4, 2, "9f3c1ab"}; constexpr toy::application::Version minimum{.major = 1, .minor = 4}; const bool supported = build >= minimum;

Construction: O(1) for the numbers; a revision built from a pointer costs one scan for the terminator. Access: O(1); every field is read directly. Equality: O(1) on the numbers, plus O(n) in the length of the revision when all three numbers match. Ordering: O(1) until the first number that differs, plus O(n) in the shorter revision when none does. Memory usage: three 32-bit numbers, then the pointer and length of the view; 32 bytes on a 64-bit target.

Lifetime: revision views characters it does not own, so the string has to outlive the version. Contracts: none of its own; revision inherits what toy::StringView checks. Memory safety: nothing allocates, and the numbers live in the object itself. Type safety: a nullptr revision meets the deleted constructor of toy::StringView and fails to compile. Exception safety: no operation throws; exceptions are off in the build. к сведению A version built without a revision compares equal only to another one that carries none. Marks T as a bit-flag enumeration the operators in this header accept; denies every type by default. The primary template leaves enable at false, so no operator applies to an arbitrary type. A full specialization setting it to true, written by hand or through ENABLE_BITWISE_OPERATORS, opts one enumeration in. Every overload constrains on toy::BitwiseEnum, which reads this value, so an enumeration that never opted in reports an unmet requirement instead of silently converting. Template Parameters T Scoped enumeration over an unsigned underlying type other than bool, whose enumerators name single bits. The primary template accepts any type; a specialization grants operators only to a type that toy::BitwiseEnum also accepts.

Opt-in per type: One specialization enables the whole operator set for one enumeration. Any named namespace: ENABLE_BITWISE_OPERATORS makes the operators reachable by argument-dependent lookup, so call sites need no using-directive. Type safety: Operands and results keep type T; the underlying integer never reaches the call site. Membership tests: toy::hasAny() and toy::hasAll() test a mask without spelling the comparison against T{}. Constexpr support: Every operator evaluates in a constant expression. No allocation: Each operator forwards to one integer operation on the underlying type.

#include "core.hpp" namespace game { enum class Flags : unsigned { none = 0u, a = 1u, b = 2u, c = 4u }; } // namespace game ENABLE_BITWISE_OPERATORS(game, Flags) constexpr game::Flags combined = game::Flags::a | game::Flags::b; constexpr bool carriesA = hasAny(combined, game::Flags::a); constexpr bool carriesAAndC = hasAll(combined, game::Flags::a | game::Flags::c);
Trait: resolved during compilation; it holds one static constexpr member and no state. Each operator: O(1), one integer operation after inlining.

Contracts: none checked. The trait does not test whether the enumerators of T occupy disjoint bits, so overlapping values stay a logic error no diagnostic reports. Type safety: participation is a requires clause, so an enumeration without a specialization, or over a signed or bool underlying type, fails to compile at the call site. Value range: a result may hold a bit pattern no enumerator names. That is well defined, because T fixes its underlying type. Exception safety: no operation throws; every operator is noexcept, and exceptions are off in the build. внимание The operators live in namespace toy, and ENABLE_BITWISE_OPERATORS adds using-declarations of them to the namespace of the enumeration, where argument-dependent lookup finds them. A specialization written by hand adds none, so for an enumeration outside toy the call site needs using namespace toy; or a using-declaration per operator. Let's discover Docusaurus in less than 5 minutes.
Get started by creating a new site. Or try Docusaurus immediately with docusaurus.new.
Node.js version 20.0 or above: When installing Node.js, you are recommended to check all checkboxes related to dependencies.

Generate a new Docusaurus site using the classic template. The classic template will automatically be added to your project after you run the command: npm init docusaurus@latest my-website classic You can type this command into Command Prompt, Powershell, Terminal, or any other integrated terminal of your code editor. The command also installs all necessary dependencies you need to run Docusaurus.

Run the development server: cd my-website npm run start The cd command changes the directory you're working with. In order to work with your newly created Docusaurus site, you'll need to navigate the terminal there. The npm run start command builds your website locally and serves it through a development server, ready for you to view at http://localhost:3000/. Open docs/intro.md (this page) and edit some lines: the site reloads automatically and displays your changes.
